title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Distribution without underwriting discipline is just a faster way to misprice credit.
epigraph.author: Consumer Finance Operating Principle

web_blocks.html: Branch-heavy universal banks rely on physical real estate to gather deposits and cross-sell products. Capital One instead runs a hybrid digital-first distribution machine powered by its AWS cloud-native core [9]. In Credit Card, acquisition flows through three main funnels. First, algorithmic direct-to-consumer digital and pre-screened mail campaigns build on Information-Based Strategy (IBS) [11]. Second, affiliate marketplaces like Credit Karma and NerdWallet drive high-intent applicants. Third, co-brand travel and B2B ecosystems (Velocity Black and Brex) replace low-margin retail ties like Walmart, exited in 2024 [4, 10, 14]. In Consumer Banking, Capital One pairs ~260+ branches and experiential Capital One Cafés with its national Capital One 360 digital bank. It also connects to a 12,000+ auto-dealer network via Auto Navigator [20]. Commercial Banking distributes through middle-market relationship teams and Brex's software-led self-serve onboarding [4, 21].

A bank's "supply chain" is its funding stack, technology infrastructure, and payment rails. On the funding side, Capital One's raw material is $480.67 billion in total deposits as of Q3 2026. Roughly 85% are FDIC-insured retail and small-business deposits [2, 5]. That deposit base provides a structural cost-of-funds edge over wholesale-funded non-bank lenders. On the technology side, Capital One exited all eight legacy data centers by 2020 and rebuilt ~2,000 applications on AWS. This modern stack runs machine-learning credit models in milliseconds and integrates acquired portfolios—like Discover's front-book and back-book card accounts—onto a unified platform [9, 18]. On the payment-rail side, owning Discover, PULSE, and Diners Club eliminates third-party network tolls on migrated debit and credit volume. Those rails are projected to generate $1.2 billion in network synergies alongside $1.5 billion in expense synergies ($2.7 billion total pre-tax run-rate by 2027) [3, 18].

web_blocks.caption: FY2025 Audited Unit Economics Waterfall ($ Millions, Bank-Adapted P&L & Cash Conversion)
web_blocks.takeaway: On $53,434M of FY2025 Net Revenue (after $15,818M interest expense netted from $58,696M interest income), Credit Loss Provision ($20,655M, or 38.7% of net revenue—elevated by Day-1 Discover CECL reserves) and Non-Interest Expense ($30,498M: $12,471M compensation + $18,027M marketing/tech/integration) left $2,281M pre-tax income and $2,088M continuing-ops net income, while operating cash flow reached $27,718M ($26,140M FCF after $1,578M capex).

web_blocks.html: Interpreting the FY2025 waterfall requires banking-specific precision [1]. Interest expense ($15,818 million) is netted directly against gross interest income ($58,696 million) to reach Net Interest Income ($42,878 million). Adding $10,556 million of non-interest income yields Total Net Revenue ($53,434 million), so the top line already reflects funding costs [1]. In the waterfall above, Provision for Credit Losses ($20,655 million) serves as the direct "cost of risk" (COGS equivalent). It represented 38.7% of FY2025 net revenue, elevated by Day-1 CECL reserve builds on the $108.2 billion Discover loan book acquired in May 2025 [1, 3]. Salaries and Associate Benefits ($12,471 million) took 23.3% of net revenue. Other Non-Interest Expense ($18,027 million, or 33.7% of net revenue) included $5,884 million in marketing, tech, occupancy, intangible amortization, and Discover integration charges. Together, these costs compressed FY2025 pre-tax income to $2,281 million and GAAP continuing-operations net income to $2,088 million [1].

web_blocks.html: Examining distribution and unit economics at the cohort level shows why marketing efficiency and credit-loss discipline must be evaluated together. Traditional branch banks rely on physical foot traffic for customer acquisition. Capital One instead runs a quantitative direct-response engine. It spans pre-screened mailers, digital affiliates, Co-Brand partner funnels, Auto Navigator dealer links, and Brex's SaaS-led corporate onboarding [1, 2, 5]. Each channel is underwritten to a strict lifetime-value-to-acquisition-cost hurdle. Those models explicitly stress-test vintage charge-off curves under higher unemployment assumptions, preventing rapid origination growth from masking weaker marginal credit quality.

On the funding side of unit economics, Capital One's 85%-FDIC-insured retail deposit base lowers marginal cost of funds relative to wholesale-funded specialty lenders [1, 25]. Combined with automated AWS cloud credit-line management, this edge supports an 8.41% Net Interest Margin alongside 4.92% loan-loss allowance coverage [25].

Discover debit migration is complete, and credit-card volume is shifting onto proprietary rails through 2027. Every incremental basis point of net network-fee capture directly improves per-$100 pre-provision cash conversion [1, 25, 27].

book_paragraphs: To understand how Capital One actually makes money on every dollar of revenue, you and I have to translate traditional industrial unit economics into the language of banking. In a factory, you buy raw steel, pay workers to stamp it, and sell a finished car. At Capital One, the raw material is $480.7 billion of deposits, the factory floor is an AWS cloud-native underwriting engine, and the finished product is a credit card swipe, an auto loan, or a commercial credit line.

Look closely at the FY2025 audited waterfall. Capital One collected $58.7 billion in gross interest income, paid $15.8 billion in interest expense to depositors and bondholders, and added $10.6 billion in non-interest fees to arrive at $53.4 billion in net revenue. From that $53.4 billion, the single largest deduction was $20.7 billion in credit loss provisions—essentially the bank's upfront reserve for borrowers who will not pay them back. Another $12.5 billion went to employee compensation and $18.0 billion to marketing, technology, and merger integration, leaving just $2.1 billion in GAAP net income.

At first glance, a 4% GAAP net margin in FY2025 looks razor-thin. But that is an accounting illusion created by CECL and M&A timing. When Capital One closed the Discover deal in May 2025, accounting rules forced it to book lifetime expected credit losses on Discover's $108.2 billion loan book immediately on Day 1, while integration charges hit operating expenses. Notice the telltale clue on the cash flow statement: Capital One generated $27.7 billion in operating cash flow in FY2025 against just $1.6 billion in capital expenditures. Once those Day-1 reserve builds normalized in 2026, Q3 2026 net interest margin surged to 8.41% and adjusted efficiency dropped to 48.76%—showing you the true earnings power of a deposit-funded, closed-loop card franchise.

Let us trace a single $100 of revenue through Capital One's FY2025 audited income statement so you can see where the cash actually lands. Out of $53,434 million in net revenue, credit losses—the $20,655 million provision for credit losses—consume nearly $38.66 of every $100 before a single employee is paid or a single marketing mailer goes out. That single line item is the heartbeat of unit economics in consumer finance. Employee compensation takes another $23.34 per $100, and other operating expenses—including heavy brand marketing, technology amortization, and Discover integration spending—absorb $33.74 per $100. What remains is $4.27 of pre-tax income and $3.91 of GAAP net income per $100 in a heavy merger-and-reserve year like FY2025, even while operating cash flow reached $27,718 million before $1,578 million of capital expenditures.

Why does that matter for your unit-economics mental model? Because Capital One's acquisition of Discover changes the plumbing of every debit and credit swipe. Previously, Capital One paid Visa and Mastercard network assessment fees on every dollar of purchase volume. By migrating Capital One's consumer debit portfolio onto Discover's PULSE network by mid-2026 and progressively shifting eligible credit volume onto the Discover Global Network, Capital One captures the merchant acquirer/network spread under the Durbin Amendment exemption for three-party networks. Every basis point saved on network rails drops straight into pre-provision earnings once the upfront integration and marketing investments taper.

Unit economics in banking are deceptive because revenue arrives upfront in the form of interest and fees, while credit losses arrive months or years later. That is why our FY2025 $100 waterfall is so illuminating. Out of every $100 of net revenue ($53,434 million total), Capital One set aside $38.66 ($20,655 million) for credit loss provisions, paid $23.34 ($12,471 million) in employee compensation, and spent $33.74 ($18,027 million) on marketing, technology, and integration overhead. Only $4.27 per $100 reached pre-tax income in that heavy merger-closing year—even as operating cash flow hit $27,718 million.

Now look at what happens to that $100 waterfall as Discover's payment rails scale. Historically, every time a Capital One customer tapped a debit or credit card at a grocery store or airline, Visa or Mastercard took a network assessment cut. By migrating Capital One's consumer debit cards onto Discover's PULSE network by mid-2026, Capital One keeps that network economics inside the family under the Durbin Amendment's three-party network exemption. That is not a one-time accounting trick; it is a permanent structural improvement in per-swipe unit economics.

Think about the difference between a two-party card issuer and a three-party closed-loop network in plain dollars and cents. When a bank issues only Visa or Mastercard cards, it is essentially renting someone else's highway and paying a toll on every mile driven. By buying Discover and migrating its debit cards onto PULSE by mid-2026, Capital One now owns the highway itself—and under the Durbin Amendment, three-party networks enjoy structural interchange exemptions that two-party bank issuers do not.

That is why the $2.7 billion pre-tax synergy target by 2027 is not just headcount trimming or overlapping office leases. A large share of those savings comes from shifting billions of dollars of debit and credit purchase volume onto proprietary rails where Capital One keeps both sides of the transaction economics.

Every basis point in consumer finance compounds enormously at Capital One's scale. On a $672.9 billion balance sheet, a 40-basis-point expansion in Net Interest Margin—like the jump to 8.41% we saw in Q3 2026—translates into billions of dollars of annualized net interest income before a single new branch is opened.

The flip side of that operating leverage is equally important for you to remember: if credit losses rise by 100 basis points across a massive card portfolio, provisions eat into pre-provision earnings just as quickly. That is why unit-economics discipline at origination is everything.

Ultimately, the beauty of tracing a $100 revenue waterfall is that it strips away corporate jargon and shows you the exact levers that move earnings: credit provisions, marketing efficiency, technology leverage, and network-fee retention.

When network-fee retention on PULSE and Discover scales alongside disciplined customer-acquisition spend, the cash-conversion efficiency of every marginal revenue dollar improves materially over time.

book_callouts.title: Reading Bank Cash Flow vs. GAAP Earnings
book_callouts.text: Why FY2025 GAAP net income ($2.09B) diverged so sharply from Operating Cash Flow ($27.72B):
bullets: CECL Day-1 Reserve Builds: Non-cash credit loss provisions ($20.66B) are expensed upfront before actual cash charge-offs occur.
Cloud-Native Capex Discipline: Capital One spent just $1.58B on premises and equipment in FY2025 because its core compute runs on AWS.
Marketing as Growth Capex: $5.88B in FY2025 marketing is expensed immediately on the P&L, even though prime cardholders stay active for 7–10+ years.
